scams.name: Fake Discount Theme Park Tickets
scams.tldr: Tickets advertised 30 to 50 percent below gate prices near the theme parks are often partially used passes, expired tickets, or counterfeits, leaving buyers turned away at the gate after paying $200 to $400.
scams.description:
Fake theme park tickets sit at the top of nearly every list of Orlando travel scams, and for good reason. Billboards, signs, and kiosks near the theme parks advertise tickets at 30 to 50 percent below gate prices, but the sellers are pushing partially used multi-day passes, expired tickets, or outright counterfeits. Victims arrive at the Disney, Universal, or SeaWorld gates only to be turned away after waiting in line for an hour, having already paid $200 to $400 for worthless tickets.

It is a misdemeanor crime in Florida for anyone to sell or transfer used multi-day theme park tickets. A telltale sign of fraud is when a seller along International Drive hands tourists a "script" telling them what to say if they are questioned at the park entrance; no legitimate ticket comes with a cover story.

The Orange County Sheriff's Department has issued official warnings about these operations and recommends buying all tickets directly from Disney, Universal, SeaWorld, or their authorized resellers. Legitimate authorized resellers display the official "Authorized Ticket Seller" logo on their websites. Newer scams in 2025 involve AI-generated fake tickets that look increasingly convincing, complete with QR codes that lead to fraudulent confirmation pages.
scams.avoidance: Buy tickets only from official park websites (disneyworld.disney.go.com, universalorlando.com) or verified authorized resellers like Undercover Tourist or Official Ticket Center. Look for the official "Authorized Ticket Seller" logo on any third-party seller's website. Never buy tickets from individuals on Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, or from hotel lobby kiosks without verified authorization. If a deal seems too good to be true, it is; Disney and Universal tightly control their pricing, and genuine discounts rarely exceed 10 to 15 percent. For significant savings, buy multi-day tickets directly from the parks (the per-day cost drops with more days) or use membership programs like AAA for verified small discounts.
scams.location: Ticket kiosks along International Drive (I-Drive), booths on Route 192 (Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway), hotel lobby ticket desks in Kissimmee, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist listings

scams.name: Timeshare Presentation Trap
scams.tldr: Companies dangle "free" stays, discounted tickets, or $100 to $200 gift cards for a "90-minute" presentation that runs three to four hours of high-pressure closers pushing $20,000 to $80,000 timeshares.
scams.description:
Orlando's timeshare presentation system is a trap that visitors walk into freely. Companies offer "free" resort stays, discounted theme park tickets, or gift cards worth $100 to $200 in exchange for attending a "90-minute presentation." The hidden cost is your time: presentations routinely last three to four hours, run by aggressive sales staff who cycle through increasingly forceful closers. Travelers report sessions billed as "90 minutes" that stretched to nearly four hours with a very hard sell and very aggressive sales staff.

The psychological manipulation follows a script. Salespeople build a personal relationship, show you dream-vacation slides, then present payment plans as "investments" costing $20,000 to $80,000, with maintenance fees of $1,000 to $2,000 annually. When you say no, a "closer" arrives offering a "special deal" available "today only." On the Disney discussion forums, longtime visitors warn that free Disney tickets through timeshare presentations haven't been available in decades; the actual offer is typically a discounted hotel room, not park tickets.

Attending a presentation can occasionally lead to free Universal Studios tickets, but the psychological pressure is extreme and designed to make people-pleasers feel unable to refuse. The pitch targets couples and families, who are more susceptible to "imagine your family vacationing here every year" emotional manipulation.
scams.avoidance: Never accept free ticket offers that require attending any kind of presentation; the value of your vacation time exceeds any freebie. If you choose to attend, set a firm 90-minute timer on your phone and stand up to leave when it rings, regardless of where the presentation stands. Bring a single phrase and repeat it: "Thank you, but no. We are not interested." Do not explain or justify your decision. Never provide credit card information "just to hold your spot" or sign any documents during the presentation. Report aggressive timeshare operations to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services at 1-800-435-7352.
scams.location: Kiosks on International Drive, Westgate Resorts presentation centers, promotional booths at Orlando Premium Outlets, hotel lobby solicitors in Kissimmee and Lake Buena Vista

scams.name: Vacation Rental Phantom Listing
scams.tldr: Scammers clone real Airbnb listings or post fake vacation homes near Disney priced 30 to 40 percent below market, collect deposits via Venmo, Zelle, or wire, then vanish, leaving families with no house, no keys, and no refund.
scams.description:
Florida has seen a wave of vacation rental scams in which families arrive in the Orlando area to find their prepaid rental homes either did not exist or belonged to different owners. The problem is growing as scammers hijack legitimate Airbnb listings, copying photos and descriptions to create duplicate ads on other platforms, then collecting deposits through Venmo, Zelle, or wire transfers.

Some Orlando Airbnb listings intentionally offer a different, lower-quality property in a less desirable location, hoping visitors will accept the switch rather than deal with finding alternative housing on arrival. The scale of the fraud is significant: the Federal Trade Commission received nearly 10,000 fraud reports in the second quarter of 2025, with scammers stealing $40 million through fake rental listings, $5 million more than the prior year.

The pattern is consistent. Scammers create attractive listings for vacation homes near Disney World priced 30 to 40 percent below comparable properties, request full payment or large deposits through peer-to-peer apps, then vanish. Families arrive after traveling across the country only to find no house, no keys, and no refund. Multiple families have been left without lodging on arrival during peak holiday seasons.
scams.avoidance: Book exclusively through Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com using only the platform's payment system, which offers refund protection if the listing is fraudulent. Verify the property has a valid Florida vacation rental license by searching at myfloridalicense.com. Never move communication or payment off-platform, even if the host offers a significant discount for direct booking. Cross-reference the property address on Google Maps Street View to verify the home exists and matches the listing photos. Book from hosts with 20 or more verified reviews across multiple months; avoid newly created listings with no review history.
scams.location: Online listings for Kissimmee vacation homes, Davenport resort communities, Champions Gate area, Facebook and Craigslist vacation rental ads

scams.name: Pizza Flyer Credit Card Phishing
scams.tldr: Realistic pizza takeout menus slipped under hotel doors capture your credit card number when you call to order; newer versions add phishing QR codes and fake "Disney Parking" payment texts.
scams.description:
The pizza flyer scam has persisted for years and remains active across Orlando's hotels. Scammers slip realistic-looking takeout menus under hotel room doors advertising pizza delivery at attractive prices. The menus feature professional graphics, fake restaurant names, and local phone numbers. When guests call to order and provide their credit card number, the scammers capture the card details for fraudulent purchases.

The scam was still going strong in 2025 and 2026, with new variants including QR codes on the flyers that lead to phishing websites. A "smishing" (SMS phishing) variant has also emerged in which fake text messages claim to be from "Disney Parking," demanding payment for a parking violation through a fraudulent link.

The scam works because tired families returning to their hotel rooms after long park days are hungry, and the convenience of pizza delivery is appealing. The flyers look professional enough to pass casual inspection, but no legitimate pizzeria slips menus under hotel room doors. Disney resort hotels explicitly prohibit solicitation in their hallways.
scams.avoidance: Never order food from menus slipped under your hotel door; use the hotel's room service, front desk recommendations, or delivery apps like Uber Eats or DoorDash. Do not call phone numbers on unsolicited flyers or click links in unexpected text messages about parking fines or resort charges. Verify any charges or fines by calling the hotel front desk directly or visiting in person rather than using numbers from flyers or texts. Report suspicious flyers to hotel management and Disney or Universal security if you are at a resort property. Use mobile ordering through the official park apps (My Disney Experience, Universal Orlando) for food within the parks.
scams.location: Disney World resort hotels, Kissimmee and Lake Buena Vista hotels, Orlando hotel corridors along I-Drive, Universal area hotel rooms

scams.name: Parking Lot Grifters and Ticket Scalpers
scams.tldr: In theme park lots and at roadside stands, grifters demand $10 to $20 to "watch your car," push partially used or timeshare-tied passes, sneak you in on their own annual pass, or sell empty Disney gift cards at a fake 20 percent discount.
scams.description:
Parking lot grifters approach tourists in theme park parking lots with a range of pitches: offering to "watch your car" for $10 to $20 (implying it will be damaged if you refuse), selling "leftover" park tickets at a discount, or claiming to be stranded families needing gas money. The tactic of implying your car is not safe unless you pay is particularly effective because tourists have rental cars full of luggage and purchases.

At roadside stands advertising "discounted tickets to local attractions," sellers use high-pressure tactics, shouting "Only one left at this price!" or "Buy now or lose your chance!" The tickets are typically bundled with mandatory timeshare attendance, or are partially used passes that may not work. Some scalpers outside the parks sell "Annual Pass" entries where they accompany you into the park using their own pass, a practice that violates park policies and can get both parties banned.

Another variant is the "gift card kiosk" scam at tourist rest stops, where sellers offer Disney gift cards at a "20% discount" that are either empty or loaded with a fraction of the stated value. When scanned at Disney, the cards show a $0 balance, and the tourist has no recourse because the purchase was cash-only from an unauthorized vendor.
scams.avoidance: Ignore all solicitors in parking lots and keep walking; do not engage in conversation or make eye contact. Park only in official theme park lots or verified parking garages; never pay an individual to "watch" your car. Buy Disney gift cards only from authorized retailers like Target, Sam's Club, or Disney.com for verified balances. Report aggressive solicitors to theme park security or the Orange County Sheriff's Office at (407) 254-7000. Lock all valuables in the trunk before arriving at parking lots; do not leave bags or electronics visible in the car.
scams.location: Parking lots along International Drive, Disney Springs parking structures, Universal CityWalk entrance areas, rest stops on I-4 near theme park exits

scams.name: Fake Rideshare and Airport Shuttle
scams.tldr: Unlicensed drivers and fake Uber and Lyft vehicles at Orlando International Airport flash printed rideshare logos, charge two to three times the app rate in cash, and sometimes detour tourists to ATMs; prepaid shuttle bookings can also vanish.
scams.description:
Unlicensed drivers operate at Orlando International Airport, approaching arriving tourists in the baggage claim area and offering "cheaper" rides to hotels and theme parks. These drivers do not carry commercial insurance, charge rates that are often higher than legitimate Uber or Lyft rides, and in some cases have driven tourists to ATMs under the pretense of needing to "get change."

Some companies, such as "Affordable Travel of Orlando LLC," offer shuttle packages online that are either not honored on arrival or involve a bait-and-switch with poorly maintained vehicles. Some tourists prepaid $50 to $80 for airport transfers only to find no driver waiting, no response from the company, and no refund.

Recent 2025 warnings include fake Uber and Lyft vehicles whose drivers display printed rideshare logos but are not connected to any platform. They accept cash payments and charge two to three times the legitimate app rate. MCO has designated rideshare pickup zones on Level 2 of the terminal garages specifically to combat this issue, but some fake drivers still approach tourists before they reach the official zone.
scams.avoidance: Always request rides through the official Uber or Lyft app and verify the driver's name, car make, model, color, and license plate before getting in. Use only MCO's designated rideshare pickup zones on Level 2 of the terminal garages; never accept rides from inside the terminal. For airport shuttles, book through your hotel or verified services like Mears Connect with confirmed pickup and tracking. Disney resort guests should use the complimentary Mears Connect or Disney's Magical Express replacement services. Report unlicensed drivers to the Orlando Police Department at (321) 235-5300 and through Uber and Lyft's in-app safety features.
scams.location: Orlando International Airport (MCO) arrivals area, Disney Springs rideshare pickup zones, Universal CityWalk exit, hotel loading zones along I-Drive
